t:
Section 307, as so redesignated in section 105(a)(3), is amended to read as follows:


“powers of the commission
“Sec. 307. (a) The Commission has the power—

“(1) 
to require by special or general orders, any person to submit, under oath, such written reports and answers to questions as the Commission may prescribe;


“(2) 
to administer oaths or affirmations;



“(3) 
to require by subpena, signed by the chairman or the vice chairman, the attendance and testimony of witnesses and the production of all documentary evidence relating to the execution of its duties;


“(4) 
in any proceeding or investigation, to order testimony to be taken by deposition before any person who is designated by the Commission and has the power to administer oaths and, in such instances, to compel testimony and the production of evidence in the same manner as authorized under paragraph (3);


“(5) 
to pay witnesses the same fees and mileage as are paid in like circumstances in the courts of the United States;


“(6) 
to initiate (through civil actions for injunctive, declaratory, or other appropriate relief), defend (in the case of any civil action brought under section 309(a)(8) of this Act) or appeal any civil action in the name of the Commission to enforce the provisions of this Act and chapter 95 and chapter 96 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, through its general counsel; 


“(7) 
to render advisory opinions under section 308 of this Act;


“(8) 
to develop such prescribed forms and to make, amend, and repeal such rules, pursuant to the provisions of chapter 5 of title 5, United States Code, as are necessary to carry out the provisions of this Act and chapter 95 and chapter 96 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954; and

“(9) to conduct investigations and hearings expeditiously, to encourage voluntary compliance, and to report apparent violations to the appropriate law enforcement authorities.

“(b) 
Upon petition by the Commission, any United States district court within the jurisdiction of which any inquiry is being carried on may, in case of refusal to obey a subpena or order of the Commission issued under subsection (a), issue an order requiring compliance. Any failure to obey the order of the court may be punished by the court as a contempt thereof.
“(c) 
No person shall be subject to civil liability to any person (other than the Commission or the United States) for disclosing information at the request of the Commission.

“(d)(1) Whenever the Commission submits any budget estimate or request to the President or the Office of Management and Budget, it shall concurrently transmit a copy of such estimate or request to the Congress.

“(2) 
Whenever the Commission submits any legislative recommendation, or testimony, or comments on legislation, requested by the Congress or by any Member of the Congress, to the President or the Office of Management and Budget, it shall concurrently transmit a copy thereof to the Congress or to the Member requesting the same. No officer or agency of the United States shall have any authority to require the Commission to submit its legislative recommendations, testimony, or comments on legislation, to any office or agency of the United States for approval, comments, or review, prior to the submission of such recommendations, testimony, or comments to the Congress.


“(e) 
Except as provided in section 309(a)(8) of this Act, the power of the Commission to initiate civil actions under subsection (a)(6) of this section shall be the exclusive civil remedy for the enforcement of the provisions of this Act.”.

fable.w: The section gives the Commission authority to make, amend, and repeal rules under chapter 5 of title 5 (the Administrative Procedure Act), which involves public notice-and-comment rulemaking, and the definition counts rulemaking authority as participation. The tempting reading is that this is only a list of internal enforcement and investigative powers (subpoenas, oaths, civil actions) plus budget and legislative transmittals to Congress, none of which would count. That reading fails because the rulemaking power in subsection (a)(8) brings the public into the Commission's decisions.
fable.s: to develop such prescribed forms and to make, amend, and repeal such rules, pursuant to the provisions of chapter 5 of title 5, United States Code, as are necessary to carry out the provisions of this Act

opus.w: The section gives the Commission authority to make rules under chapter 5 of title 5 (the Administrative Procedure Act). That brings in notice-and-comment procedures open to the public, and the definition treats rulemaking as participation. It also mentions defending suits brought by outside parties under section 309(a)(8). The opposite reading fails because, although the subpoenas and copies sent to Congress are not participation, the rulemaking power on its own is enough.
opus.s: to develop such prescribed forms and to make, amend, and repeal such rules, pursuant to the provisions of chapter 5 of title 5, United States Code, as are necessary to carry out the provisions of this Act
opus.b:
**Tempting wrong reading:** The section looks like it only lists FEC enforcement powers (subpoenas, oaths, suits brought by the Commission) and sends copies of material to Congress. Those parts stay inside the federal government or describe enforcement, not participation.

**Why that fails:** Paragraph (8) authorizes the Commission to make, amend, and repeal rules "pursuant to the provisions of chapter 5 of title 5." That is the Administrative Procedure Act, which provides for notice-and-comment rulemaking, and the definition counts rulemaking authority as participation. Paragraph (6) also refers to defending civil actions "brought under section 309(a)(8)," which suggests outside parties can sue over Commission decisions.

qwen_chat.w: This section outlines the internal powers of the Commission, such as subpoenaing witnesses, administering oaths, and initiating civil actions. It does not establish a process for outside parties (states, tribes, public, experts) to consult with or participate in federal decision-making. The mention of 'hearings' refers to the Commission's investigative or enforcement proceedings, not public participation mechanisms like comment periods or advisory boards with non-federal members. The requirement to transmit budget estimates to Congress is intra-governmental communication.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the Commission's power to "render advisory opinions" or "conduct hearings" implies public participation. However, these are internal administrative powers of the agency itself, not mechanisms for outside parties to influence federal decision-making. The "hearings" mentioned are likely investigative or enforcement hearings conducted by the Commission, not public comment periods or advisory committees with non-federal members. The section primarily defines the Commission's internal authority and its relationship with Congress and the courts.
